catalog_quote: 1.4. The Hopi Stress Rule. For the most part, stress is predictable in Hopi. Basically, the assignment of stress conforms to the following principles: (a) The second vowel, counting from the left, is stressed in polysyllabic words (i.e. words which are trisyllabic or longer) in which the first vowel is followed by a single consonant or directly by a vowel. (In calculating the length of a word, VV sequences count as disyllabic.) (b) The first vowel is stressed otherwise--i.e. in disyllabics, and in polysyllabics whose first vowel is followed by a consonant cluster. ... The first of these subrules assigns stress to polysyllabics whose first vowel is followed by a single consonant (including glide or laryngeal under the term 'consonant' here), as in (17) kiyapi 'dipper', caqapta 'dish', panapca 'window' ... and to polysyllabics whose first vowel is followed directly by another vowel--i.e. …

sources.quote: 'the acute accent to mark primary stress in those cases where it occurs contrary to the rules of the Hopi second mora stress pattern (secondary stress is left unmarked), and the grave accent to indicate falling tone.' Names the default as a second-mora pattern (= initial heavy syllable or else second syllable), consistent with the weight-sensitive left-edge coding; no rule details.

sources.quote: Mora ('unit') formulation: 'CV- one unit; CVV- two units; CVC- two units; CVC (final) one unit ... In words of two units, the stress falls on the first unit ... In words of more than two units the stress normally falls on the second unit: momoyam "women", paasa "field" ... In words of a CVCCV pattern the stress regresses to the vowel of the first unit, since a consonant cannot take the stress.' p. 519: 'There is only one primary stress in each Hopi word. Longer words have a complicated system of secondary and tertiary stress which is predictable in a complex way intentionally not discussed her
sources.note: Independent mora-based statement of the same rule plus an explicit note that secondary/tertiary stress exists but is unanalysed — fills the empty secondary-stress field's provenance (StressTyp2 cites 'Seaman 1985' for secondary stresses).
